FF7 was released on the PS1 before the dualshock controller even existed. The game pre-dates analogue joysticks on controllers on the Playstation. This game came out so early in the Playstation 1 era that when it was released everyone was blown away, literally floored, by the quality of the CGI cut scenes.

Yes, the graphics haven't ages well. The ultra low poly models are extremely dated. But that isn't fair, to judge a game from 1997 by 2015 standards. That game is over 18 years old, there are people posting on this board who are younger than that game.

As for sound, you sir can fuck right off with that nonsense. The music from FF7 is some of the best in all of gaming, there are touring orchestras that play nothing but the songs from that game. When Square released the symphonic recordings of the Final Fantasy games, more songs from FF7 are included than any other FF (with FF6 a close second).

As for the story... yes it is a complicated plot with a lot going on, but it isn't as insane as many other games, or even Final Fantasy games. There is a lot of subplot and it takes a few play throughs to really grasp what is actually going on. But the story holds up.

On of the main reasons why the story is so good IMO is because the game has one of the best villains in all of Final Fantasy, if not gaming (and your protagonists are only as quality as your antagonist). One of the reasons FF13 sucked is because there is no personified face of villainy, there is no concrete antagonist, just "the Cieth" or "fate" which is nebulous and weak. FF6 has a fantastic antagonist with Kefka, Kefka is arguably better than Sephiroth because Kefka actually accomplishes total global destruction, but FF6 falters because FF6 has no concrete protagonist, rather an ensemble cast of protagonists which leaves the story somewhat lacking in a solid relate-able anchor. FF10 has a great antagonist with Sin but its more beastly than personified also Seymour distracts from Sin's greatness and is a weaker more annoying echo of Kuja or Kefka.

But Sephiroth holds the whole world in terror. He is personal to the main characters, he becomes personal to the player after the flashbacks to Nibelheim, he wins at every step of the game until the end. Even if you don't hate him on a personal level after Nibelheim, by the end of Disc 1 you will utterly loath him.

Which brings me to why I think you played it recently for the first time. Because anyone who played it when it was first released, particularly those of us who were deeply in love with everything Squaresoft back at that time... were totally floored by the end of Disc 1, and the graphics, and the music, and the story. But people who didn't come into all that fresh. People who've been exposed to years and years of FF7 pop culture and references and THEN play the game will not see it fresh, they will see it as a contrived pixelated mess of all this irreverent oversaturated hot-topic-ish pop culture garbage.

Which is really sad, because when it was new, when none of that pop culture existed, it was mother fucking amazing.

Sephiroth is actually killed during (by Cloud) in the Nibelhiem flashback. His body (and spirit) float along the life stream and end up encased in materia at the northern crater. Cloud isn't a Sephiroth clone exactly. More of a "failed"clone project run by Hojo (on him and Zack in tandem). The lies and confusion that Cloud experiences the whole first half of the game is a combined result of Cloud's personal guilt letting Sephiroth's will manipulate him combined with his proximity to Zack. So Cloud's guilt and weakness result in him being manipulated by Sephiroth into getting the black materia and later turning it over, while using Zack as a crutch to hide his weakness behind. Mass Effect 3. The first game in the trilogy set up an interesting universe in which humanity is a fledgling spacefaring power exploring a dangerous, largely unexplored region of space and attempting to earn its place among the established civilizations of the galaxy. Mass Effect 2 expanded on this by having the player pursue enemies through the dark underbelly of the established galaxy, the Terminus Systems. The first game established the setting, the second gave it texture and variety. Both games had a consistent, interesting mythology, a more or less conventional war between the galactic civilizations and a race of intelligent robots, and a main conflict that centered around a vaguely Lovecraftian world-ending enemy that Had To Be Stopped.

Then, Mass Effect 3 came along and messed it all up. The races of the galaxy were turned into silly human archetypes, the main conflict of the first two games was stupidly retconned, and worst of all, the giant threat to the galaxy was demystified from a Cthulhu-like world ending evil to a pretty much conventional horde of cartoonishly grotesque monsters. And, once the player slogs through the (ultimately pointless) struggle to build the super weapon that will defeat the giant Cthulhu-like monsters, he or she is forced to pick between three endings that leave the universe in completely different states, making it impossible to use the setting in future games.

The Mass Effect universe started out as a basically Star Wars like setting, with some interesting and well thought out civilizations and lots of potential for adventure and exploration. It could have gone on indefinitely with new characters and adventures on all sorts of scales, anything from fighting in giant wars to setting up colonies on the edge of known space. And then they ruined it.
